items.title: [elpais.com] Cyberattacks on refrigeration systems fuel concerns about connected household appliances
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Cyberattacks on internet-connected refrigeration systems in supermarkets and French blood banks have destroyed food in Europe and heightened concerns about connected devices. Nearly 800 freezers were sabotaged in France and Northern Europe this week. On November 2, temperatures also rose in the cold rooms of a blood donation service in France. There, alarms and swift action prevented damage to stored blood. The targeted systems used internet-accessible controls for maintenance and remote operation. According to experts, similar attacks on private smart-home devices are less likely because, with typical router configurations, the devices cannot be accessed directly from the internet. Risks include outdated software, weak passwords, and devices with cameras or microphones. Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security recommends automatic updates, separate networks for smart-home devices, and unique passwords. The identity of those behind the attacks remains unclear.

Recorded access attempts: Security company Lupovis recorded more than 276 access attempts by 91 different actors against components of Danfoss control systems between October 20 and 30; activity peaked on October 26 (euronews.com). Weak security: Researchers found nearly 13,000 internet-accessible management services for refrigeration systems in 99 countries; some systems used weak or no passwords (reddit.com). Food inspections: In 2024, more than 285,000 inspections were conducted in retail stores in Spain, and over 60,000 in warehouses and distribution centers (elpais.com). Security measures: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity recommends separate networks, encrypted remote access for maintenance providers, and regular recovery tests for industrial refrigeration systems (elpais.com).

Security researchers found that 35,578 of 37,571 web apps built with SpaceXSI’s Grok Build, a chat-based app builder, were accessible without signing in, exposing business and personal information at SpaceXSI and 30 other organizations. The apps’ addresses were discoverable through searchable passive DNS records, and Grok Build preselected “Anyone with the link” as the sharing option in the researchers’ test. SpaceXSI removed 24 apps made by its own staff and X employees; Claroc said other users’ apps remained available and that it had begun contacting affected organizations.

items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [36kr.com] EU sues IBM, Atos and Leonardo over border system delays
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The European Union has sued IBM, French IT group Atos and Italian defence contractor Leonardo over repeated delays in developing its Entry/Exit System (EES), an electronic border-check system for the 29-country Schengen area. The EU agency eu-LISA filed the civil case in Estonia in December 2025; the dispute became public on Monday. The agency and the European Commission say the case concerns development delays, not the system’s current operation. The system was initially scheduled to launch in 2022 but was not fully rolled out until 2026. Its introduction caused hours-long airport queues after fingerprint scanners malfunctioned, including when exposed to sweat. Some countries are still acquiring scanners. The system records fingerprints and photographs from non-EU travellers on their first entry to help identify visa overstayers and identity fraud. eu-LISA says the case does not affect operations. Estonia’s Harju County Court has accepted the case, but no hearing has been held or scheduled.

items.title: [livescience.com] NASA's Swift telescope burns up after nearly 22 years
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña submitted his resignation on Nov. 5 as the collapse of digital lender Ueno Bank froze access to accounts held by nearly 3 million customers. He said he would appear at the Senate proceedings to defend himself. Vice President Pedro Alliana is next in line if lawmakers accept Peña’s resignation or remove him through impeachment. Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno on Nov. 3 after finding that its solvency ratio had fallen below half the required minimum. The intervention shut down the bank’s app, cards and transfers. Ueno had about 3 million customers and administered roughly $850 million in public funds, including pension-related money. Lawmakers accuse Peña of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and shielding the bank from scrutiny. He has denied wrongdoing and said the matter should be handled through the courts. Prosecutors ordered three investigations into the bank’s failure, covering oversight, the handling of its collapse and the placement of public funds.

India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned financial firms that an active campaign it calls Crafty Falcon is targeting non-bank lenders, fintech companies, payment providers and cryptocurrency exchanges. Attackers use publicly available AI-assisted tools to find exposed applications, application programming interfaces (APIs) and privileged access, then misuse victims’ own payment systems to transfer funds. CERT-In says attacks have continued against organizations that did not fully address earlier weaknesses, with intrusions timed for weekends and holidays when monitoring may be reduced. According to a police complaint, two Mumbai-based non-bank lenders lost about $2 million in more than 700 unauthorized transfers on Oct. 8 and 9 after attackers compromised APIs. Reports on that incident did not establish a link to Crafty Falcon.

items.title: [sciencefeatured.com] Higher BMI over time linked to faster cognitive decline in older adults
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Full-fat dairy may not be the health villain it has long been portrayed as, according to a new study finding that three daily servings did not worsen weight, cholesterol, or insulin resistance over 12 weeks. Researchers also observed improvements in blood pressure and nutrient intake, raising questions about longstanding recommendations to choose low-fat dairy.
